title: Good Intentions, Bad Science: The Closed Loop of Clinical Judgment
coreMove: Turn a confident helping story into a testable hypothesis before good intentions seal the loop.
sourcePressure: The chapter critiques clinical judgment when intuition and benevolent identity become a closed loop; the source emphasizes science as error exposure, arrogance control, and the danger of suggestive interviewing.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Attacking therapy, clinicians, or expertise broadly instead of targeting untested confirmation loops inside helping work.

sourceAnchors.name: arrogance control
sourceAnchors.detail: the source supports the phrase as a way to frame scientific method forcing experts to face the possibility of error
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Good method is arrogance control: it makes even the caring expert leave room to be wrong.

sourceAnchors.name: suggestive child interviews
sourceAnchors.detail: the source supports the risk that child-abuse and similar interviews become contaminated when the interviewer seeks confirmation instead of testing alternatives
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: The danger begins when a question stops searching and starts leading the witness toward the story the helper already believes.

hook: Do not open with a therapist as villain.
counterintuition: Do not imply compassion makes people less reliable by itself.
Avoid "science beats feelings" as a blunt frame.
examples: No courtroom child-abuse case details beyond the source boundary.
No medical diagnosis drama as the only clinical setting.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person direct address, retrospective realization, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm: a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.domain: a school counselor interviewing a ten-year-old after a playground injury report
exampleSpecs.audience: helpers who fear missing harm and may start leading before testing
exampleSpecs.stakes: the child's answer may become evidence shaped by the adult's first theory
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Laura writes two alternative explanations on a sticky note before asking the next question, then replaces a leading prompt with an open one
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a cartoon bandage wrapper beside a child-sized chair

exampleSpecs.domain: an addiction clinic case conference where staff read missed appointments as denial
exampleSpecs.audience: care teams whose rescue identity can close down rival hypotheses
exampleSpecs.stakes: a patient loses housing support if practical barriers are misread as resistance
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Mathieu asks the team to list what would disprove denial before they write the care plan
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a bus-transfer slip tucked into a clinic intake folder

exampleSpecs.domain: a speech-language assessment for a preschooler in a bilingual household
exampleSpecs.stakes: a child may be mislabeled because every silence is interpreted through one favored explanation
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Frida predicts what she would see if shyness, hearing trouble, or language exposure were each true, then changes the session plan
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a felt animal board lined up beside a small audiology headset

exampleSpecs.domain: a workplace investigator reviewing a harassment complaint without assuming the first narrative is complete
exampleSpecs.audience: internal investigators balancing care with verification
exampleSpecs.stakes: a flawed interview sequence could contaminate testimony and undermine real accountability
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ben deletes a question that names the alleged motive and replaces it with a sequence question about what each person saw first
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a digital recorder beside a blank chronology grid

exampleSpecs.domain: a nonprofit youth mentor interpreting a teenager's silence as trauma disclosure
exampleSpecs.audience: well-meaning mentors who need humility around interpretation
exampleSpecs.stakes: the teenager may be pushed into an adult story before trust or evidence exists
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: You watch Catarina write "maybe" beside each interpretation, then ask what the teen wants help with today instead of naming the hidden wound
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a half-finished chessboard on a community center table

exampleSpecs.domain: a hospital quality-improvement analyst checking a senior consultant's theory about readmissions
exampleSpecs.audience: analysts who must challenge confident experts without humiliating them
exampleSpecs.stakes: resources go to the wrong fix if narrative fit outranks disconfirming data
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: It takes Yusuf one cross-tab to show that the consultant's favored explanation predicts the wrong ward, then he designs a falsifying check for the next meeting
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a discharge binder opened beside a green spreadsheet filter

skillTargets: turn a clinical interpretation into a falsifiable hypothesis
spot leading questions that contaminate evidence
evaluate when good intentions are shielding a closed loop

tryThisNowSpec: For one judgment you feel sure about, write the sentence "If I am wrong, I would expect to see..." and name one observation that could actually unsettle you.
